title: Cato Amicus Brief Challenges $100,000 H-1B Fee in First Circuit Appeal
excerpt: Filed for the Cato Institute and professor Ilya Somin, the brief argues the payment is a tax only Congress can impose — while the fee itself remains vacated as the government appeals.
body:
• The Cato Institute and professor Ilya Somin filed an amicus brief on November 12 in the First Circuit, supporting California and 19 other states challenging the $100,000 H-1B payment.
  • The brief argues the payment is a tax, not a fee, and that only Congress can impose taxes — the power to restrict entry is not the power to tax entry.
  • The fee is not in effect under the challenged policy: a Massachusetts district court vacated it on June 8, 2026, and the First Circuit refused on July 24 to pause that ruling while the government appeals.
  • For employers and H-1B workers, nothing changes today — the appeal in State of California v. Mullin, No. 26-1699, will decide whether the vacatur stands, so petitions should be planned against the court's eventual ruling, not the brief.

The legal fight over the Trump administration's $100,000 payment on H-1B petitions gained a new brief this week. The Cato Institute and George Mason University law professor Ilya Somin filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit on November 12, supporting the states in State of California v. Mullin, No. 26-1699. Somin announced the filing in Reason, where he writes as part of the Volokh Conspiracy.

Who is affected

The payment at issue was imposed by Proclamation 10973, issued on September 19, 2025, which required a $100,000 payment to accompany H-1B petitions for workers outside the United States, according to the First Circuit's July 24 order in the case. H-1B visas are used by technology firms, research institutions and other employers to hire workers in specialty occupations that usually require at least a bachelor's degree. The states challenging the policy told the court it harms their ability to staff publicly run colleges and universities, schools and healthcare systems.

Workers already in the United States on other statuses, and employers whose petitions were never covered by the proclamation's terms, are not the subject of this case. The question before the First Circuit is narrower: whether the government can charge this payment at all.

What the brief argues

The brief's core claim is that the $100,000 exaction is a tax because its defining feature is that it raises revenue — it is neither a fee that recovers the cost of running the H-1B program nor a penalty. On that reading, the Constitution reserves the decision to Congress.

"The Framers gave Congress alone access to the pockets of the people."

— Cato Institute and Ilya Somin amicus brief, quoting Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump

The brief argues that the statutes the government relies on — sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which let the president restrict entry — say nothing about charging for entry, and that Congress set out H-1B fees expressly and in detail elsewhere in the same act. It notes that in more than a century no president has used those provisions to raise revenue. It then adds two fallback arguments: that claiming unlimited taxing power over visa holders raises a major question requiring a clear statement from Congress, and that if the statutes did grant the power claimed, the delegation itself would be unconstitutional.

The brief leans on the Supreme Court's decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the tariff case in which Somin participated, which held that a general power to regulate importation did not include the power to impose tariffs. Stanford law professor and former federal judge Michael McConnell worked on the brief, with Deno Himonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati acting as counsel, according to the filing.

Where the case stands

The district court in Massachusetts invalidated the payment on June 8, 2026, holding that the executive had usurped Congress's power to impose taxes, and vacated the implementing policy in its entirety. The government appealed. On July 24, 2026, a First Circuit panel denied the government's request to stay that judgment, finding it had not made a strong showing that it was likely to succeed on appeal. A second federal district court later invalidated the fee on other grounds, Somin writes.

The amicus brief is argument, not a ruling. The First Circuit has yet to decide the appeal itself.

What to do next

For now, the practical position follows the court orders, not the brief: the policy implementing the $100,000 payment stands vacated in this case, and the stay denial means that vacatur remains in place while the appeal is heard. Employers filing H-1B petitions for workers abroad, and workers expecting to be sponsored, should track the First Circuit appeal in No. 26-1699 and confirm the current collection position before filing, because a ruling for the government would revive the payment question. Anyone whose petition timing depends on the outcome should take case-specific advice rather than rely on the brief's arguments, however prominent its authors are.
